astra.text:
Yeah, so, um, that paper was about revisiting convolutional networks and asking what a modern convnet should look like. And the broader question is very related to what you just mentioned: when we make progress, which components are actually responsible for that progress?

So when we compare two models, we often describe the difference in terms of architecture. But usually there are other differences, too—the training procedure, the amount of computation, the choices you make inside each block. If you change all of those together, it becomes difficult to say which part is giving you the improvement.

The idea was to take a convolutional network and systematically modernize it, looking at those choices one by one. Can we keep convolution as the basic operation while updating the design around it? And how far can that take us?

So, to me, the interesting point is that the basic operation is only one component of the system. The details of how you put those operations together, and how you train the resulting network, also matter a lot. And that makes this a useful starting point for your question, because before deciding that one component is essential, we should try to separate its contribution from everything else that changed.

sol.text:
Yeah, sure. So the paper is called “A ConvNet for the 2020s,” and the model is ConvNeXt. At that time, vision transformers were becoming dominant, and people often attributed their success mainly to the transformer architecture. We wanted to ask a slightly different question: how much of that improvement actually comes from the architecture, and how much comes from the modern training recipe and design choices around it?

So we started with a standard ResNet and gradually modernized it using ideas that had proved effective in vision transformers—things like the stage design, larger kernels, depthwise convolutions, normalization, activation functions, and the training procedure. What we found was that a pure convolutional network, without attention, could still be extremely competitive with transformers on image classification and downstream tasks like detection and segmentation.

I think the broader lesson is that the basic operation—convolution versus attention—is only one component of an AI system. The architecture matters, of course, but the training recipe, data, optimization, scaling, and all these small design decisions can matter just as much. ConvNeXt was really an attempt to disentangle those factors and ask what we actually need from a modern vision model.

r001.rationale: The response says training recipes and design choices matter substantially, but does not clearly state that the performance gap was primarily due to design details rather than an inherent self-attention advantage.

r002.rationale: It states that a pure convolutional network could be extremely competitive with vision transformers on image classification, detection, and segmentation, covering diverse vision tasks.

opus.text:
Yeah, sure. So, um, the context back then — this was, uh, late 2021, early 2022 — was that Vision Transformers had basically taken over. ViT came out, and then Swin Transformer showed that transformers could also do detection and segmentation really well, not just ImageNet classification. And the narrative in the community was kind of, you know, "convolution is dead, attention is all you need," even for vision.

And, um, we were a little suspicious of that narrative. Because if you actually look at what changed, it wasn't just the attention mechanism. The training recipes changed a lot at the same time — people went from, like, 90 epochs with SGD to 300 epochs with AdamW, heavy augmentation, Mixup, CutMix, RandAugment, stochastic depth, all of that. And the macro design changed too. So the comparison was never really apples to apples.

So what we did in ConvNeXt was, uh, kind of a controlled study. We started from a vanilla ResNet-50 and we just modernized it step by step, and at every step we reported the number. So first just the training recipe — that alone took ResNet-50 from about 76 to 78.8, which is already, you know, a huge chunk of the gap right there. And then we changed the stage compute ratio to match Swin, we used a patchify stem, depthwise convolutions, inverted bottleneck, larger kernels — seven by seven — fewer normalization layers, LayerNorm instead of BatchNorm, GELU instead of ReLU. Each one is a small delta.

And at the end you get a pure ConvNet that matches or beats Swin Transformer at every scale, same FLOPs, on ImageNet and on COCO and ADE20K. The biggest model got to 87.8% top-1.

Um, but I think the paper is often misread as "convolutions win." That's not really the point. The point is more that the architecture was carrying much less of the credit than people assumed. A lot of what looked like an architectural revolution was, uh, training recipes and scale. And I think that observation generalizes pretty far beyond vision.

r001.rationale: The response explains that training recipes, scaling, and architectural design changes—not an inherent superiority of attention—accounted for much of the apparent gap, explicitly saying architecture carried less credit than assumed.

r002.rationale: It states that the modernized pure ConvNet matched or beat Swin Transformer at every scale and on ImageNet, COCO, and ADE20K.

grok.text:
Yeah, sure. So that paper is A ConvNet for the 2020s — ConvNeXt. This was around the time Vision Transformers were taking over, and a lot of people had the sense that ConvNets were kind of done, and that attention was the thing that made modern vision models work.

What we actually did was pretty simple. We started from a standard ResNet and modernized it step by step, borrowing the design choices that people were using in ViTs and Swin — the training recipe, the stage compute ratio, a patchify stem, depthwise convolutions, inverted bottlenecks, larger kernels, GELU, LayerNorm, fewer activation and normalization layers, and so on. The point was not to invent a totally new architecture. It was to ask: if you give a ConvNet the same modern treatment, how far can it go?

And it turned out a pure ConvNet, with no attention at all, could match or even beat hierarchical Vision Transformers on ImageNet and on downstream tasks. So a lot of what looked like a Transformer advantage was really about training and these architecture details, not the attention mechanism itself.

That is a useful way to start thinking about today’s systems more generally. There are a few components people treat as load-bearing — the backbone, the training recipe, the inductive bias, the data, the scaling — and it is not always obvious which ones are actually doing the work, and which ones are more interchangeable than they look.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly says the apparent Transformer advantage was due to training and architecture details, not the attention mechanism itself.

r002.rationale: It states that a modernized pure ConvNet could match or outperform hierarchical Vision Transformers on ImageNet and downstream tasks.

gemini.text:
Yeah, sure. So that paper is about ConvNeXt, which came out around late 2021. At that time, Vision Transformers—like ViT and Swin Transformer—were really taking over computer vision, and a lot of people were starting to believe that maybe ConvNets were obsolete and attention mechanisms were just fundamentally better for vision tasks.

So we wanted to ask a fundamental question: is the success of Vision Transformers really coming from self-attention itself, or is it largely due to modern architectural design choices and updated training techniques that standard ConvNets, like ResNet from 2015, simply hadn't incorporated yet?

What we did was we started with a standard ResNet and gradually "modernized" it step-by-step, borrowing ideas and design choices from Transformers—things like macro design changes, inverted bottlenecks, larger kernel depthwise convolutions, using GELU instead of ReLU, fewer normalization layers, and modern training recipes. And what we found was that by just adopting these modern design decisions, a pure ConvNet—which we called ConvNeXt—could match or even outperform Swin Transformer across various vision tasks, while maintaining the simplicity and efficiency of traditional ConvNets.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly says the gap was largely due to modern architectural and training choices, rather than an inherent superiority of self-attention over convolution.

r002.rationale: It states that the modernized ConvNeXt could match or outperform Swin Transformer across various vision tasks.

kimi.text:
Yeah, sure. So, this paper is called "A ConvNet for the 2020s" — we also call it ConvNeXt. The motivation was that around that time, vision Transformers had started to dominate computer vision. Swin Transformer came out, and it was hierarchical, it was very strong, and people were saying, okay, convolution is basically dead, Transformers are going to take over everything.

So the question we wanted to ask was: is the success of these models really coming from the self-attention mechanism itself, or is it coming from a lot of the other things that were introduced along the way — like the modern training recipes, the architectural design choices, the normalization layers, and so on?

So what we did is we started from a standard ResNet, trained with a standard recipe, and then we gradually modernized it, step by step, borrowing design elements from the Swin Transformer. Things like the improved training procedure, larger kernel sizes, depthwise convolutions, inverted bottleneck blocks, using LayerNorm instead of BatchNorm, fewer activation functions and normalization layers — stuff like that. And at every step, the performance went up.

And in the end, we got a purely convolutional network — there's no attention in it at all — that could match or even outperform Swin Transformers of similar size on ImageNet and on downstream tasks like detection and segmentation.

So I think the takeaway there is that a lot of the gains people attributed to attention actually come from these components — the training recipe, the block design, the overall architecture. And if you give a ConvNet the same modern treatment, it's still very competitive. Which I think relates to what you want to talk about — decomposing what actually matters in today's AI systems.

r001.rationale: The response explains that gains attributed to self-attention largely came from modern training recipes, architectural choices, normalization, and block design rather than an inherent advantage of attention over convolution.

r002.rationale: It states that a purely convolutional network matched or outperformed similarly sized Swin Transformers on ImageNet and downstream detection and segmentation tasks.

fable.text:
Sure, yeah. So that paper, ConvNeXt, we did it at, uh, at Meta, at FAIR, back in 2021, early 2022. And the motivation was basically, at that time, Vision Transformers were, you know, taking over everything in computer vision. First ViT, and then Swin Transformer, which was, uh, kind of a hierarchical transformer that worked really well for detection, segmentation, all these downstream tasks. And everyone was sort of saying, okay, ConvNets are done, attention is the thing.

But we had a question, which is, where does the improvement actually come from? Because when you compare a Swin Transformer to a ResNet-50, you are not just changing convolution to attention. You are changing the training recipe, the optimizer, the data augmentation, the normalization, the block design, the, uh, the stem, everything. So it's not really a controlled comparison.

So what we did is, we started from a standard ResNet-50, and we gradually "modernized" it, step by step, toward the design of a Swin Transformer, but we never added attention. So the first step is just the training recipe. Use AdamW, train longer, 300 epochs, use Mixup, CutMix, RandAugment, stochastic depth, label smoothing, all these things. And just that, uh, takes ResNet-50 from like 76 to 78 or 79 percent on ImageNet. So already a big chunk of the gap is closed, and you haven't touched the architecture.

Then we go through the macro design. So change the stage ratio to something like three, three, nine, three, like Swin. Replace the stem with a patchify layer, so a four by four conv with stride four, kind of like the patch embedding. Then we, uh, ResNeXt-ify it with depthwise convolution, use an inverted bottleneck like in MobileNet or the MLP block in transformers, and then use a large kernel, seven by seven, instead of three by three. Because if you think about it, attention has a global receptive field, and a depthwise conv with a big kernel is kind of, um, a cheap way to get a larger receptive field.

And then micro design. ReLU to GELU, fewer activation functions, fewer normalization layers, BatchNorm to LayerNorm, separate downsampling layers. Each one of these gives you maybe a few tenths of a percent, but they add up.

And at the end, you have a pure ConvNet, no attention anywhere, that matches or slightly outperforms Swin on ImageNet, and also on COCO and ADE20K, while being, uh, simpler and often faster, because it's just convolutions.

So I think the message of the paper was not really "ConvNets are better than transformers." The message was more like, a lot of what we attribute to the architecture is actually coming from these other components, the recipe, the design details. And, uh, that's kind of the mindset I've had in a lot of my work since then. Just try to isolate what actually matters.

r001.rationale: The response explains that much of the apparent transformer advantage came from training recipes and architectural design details, rather than attention itself.

r002.rationale: It states that the modernized pure ConvNet matched or slightly outperformed Swin on ImageNet, COCO, and ADE20K, covering multiple vision tasks.
